PEACE MEETING AT WARRINGTON, Mn. MoM t a NIES ON THE WAR CRISI On -Wednesday night Mr. W. Pollard delivered a ; actors under the auspices of the International Arbi- ration Aseeciation,-aaffie Public Hall. Warrington, under the presidency of /11r. J. G. Dlcalinnies, J.P. There were present on the platform Mr. Joha Cros- field, J.P., Dr. Smith, J.P., D. Gornall, Mr. P. T. Winskill, Coot oilier Dixon, Mr. H. Roberts, arc., Scc. There woe a tolerably good attendance. The CIikIEALLY, whe was loudly applauded, said: Gentlemen, the title of the address that we are as- sembled to listen to to-night, will bring to the minds of many of us present the gigantic blunder of the Crimean war. (Hear, hear.) We shall remember the passions and prejudices, the ignorance, and the unrea- senable antipathies and partialities that led to that war, and we shall remember the great story of disas- ter and humiliation that attended its continuance and its conclusion. I suppose there never was a more popu- lar war, and I suppose there never was a war of which everybody now living in England is more ashamed. (Hear, hear.) We were told as a motive for that war in the first place that the Turk could be reclaimed and made a decent member of the European family. Lord Palmerston preached this doctrine, and I am sorry to believe that Lord Palmerston did not believe the doctrine he preached, and I have no doubt he said this In order to get a certain amount of support for the policy he was determined to pursue, even to the bitter end of a war with Russia. Other people told us that it was desirable to humble Russia, and then other people told us that as we had not had a war for forty years it was desirable for our prestige, and in order to show that our attention to the material interests ot the kingdom had not made us an unwarlike nation, we should go to war at once with Russia. (Hear hear.) We had at the head of the Government :at that time a Tory nobleman, Lord Aberdeen, and I believe he was sincerely opposed to the war, and extremely anxious to preserve peace. He was, however, rather a weak man, and he allowed himself to be governed by other people, and so somehow or other we drifted into war. Now, whatever the reasons were, and I suppose I have mentioned them, that instigated this country to go into war—and certainly the country was determined to do it, for there never was a time when the country was so fearfully and wonderfully mad—whatever those reasons were, the result of the war has shown that it was utterly false and foolish. (Cheers.) The Turks are not regenerated, they are in fact at this moment as utterly and completely corrupt and depraved as they were at the time when Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright told us that they were entirely beyond ref (aim. (Hear, hear.) Russia was not humiliated by that war. On the contrary, I believe at the present time they cone sider the defence of Sebaste,pol against the allied armies; as the proudest page in their military history. The prestige of Englatid as a warlike nation was not ! raised, so far from tb:at I believe that we lost what re- putation we had gained by the success of our wars with the First Napoleon, and so far as any reasons which were given at that time for entering into war, they have been found to be entirely delusive. (Hear, hear.) Instead of any reputation being gained by the English army there seems to be not a single gleam of good fortuom that can compensate for the disas era we suffered during that war, such for instance as the failure our navy, the starvation of our army, and that w onderful disaster, the bloody blunder of Bala- claws. (Cheers.) Now, I believe that a few months ago it was the intention of the present Prime Minister of England to lead us into a similar war, for the ad- vantage of the Turk and against Russia. (Hear, hear.) He has no policy of his own' he is no states- man, and he took up the polies, of Lord Palmerston, a policy which was a blunder then and has been proved to be so since. (Laughter.) There can be no doubt at all that that foolish speech that he made at Guildhall not long ego was intended by him to exas- perate the Emperor of Russia, and when we remember that at the time he made that speech he was actually suppressing a despatch which showed the panific intentions of the s mperor of Russia towards this country, there can be no doubt at all that you are hardly employing too strong a phrase when you characterise that speech as positively diaboli- cal. (Cheers.) I believe, myself, that Lord Beacons- field at that time and for many months pre- viously, was anxious to figure in the history of this country as Prime Minister of England during a long and bloody war with Russia. (Hear, tear.) This seems atrery hard speech, but a man who will deride and sneer at whet we call the Bulgarian atrocities is a man that will do anything. (Cheers.) I have no doubt at all in my own mind that the desire of Lord Beaconsfield has been to identify himself with a page in history that would make him remembered. I believe that there is no chance at the preeent time of this country going to war in favour of the Turk upon any pretext whatever. (Cheers.) That business has been nettled. (Hear, hear.) It was settled by the meetings that were held throughout this country some weeks ago. (Cheers.) I be- lieve also that the attempt to excite a jealousy and hatred of this country against Russia, and thereby to promote war, has been equally checkmated. (Cheers.) There is no doubt this attempt was made by certain cliques in London, and by certain newspapers published in the metropolis; but I believe that those cliques and newspapers, unless they are very hard learners, are now beginning to learn that whatever in- fluence they may have in London, they have very little influence in the provinces. (Cheers.) For anythingl i know, the ,Pall Mall Gazette is very largely read n London, but it is very little read amongst the five millions of the population of Lancashire and York- ehire, and it has very little influence. (Cheers.) It is a great misfortune, no doubt, that at the present juncture we should be governed by a Prime Minister like Lord Beaconsfield—(hear, hear)—and that we should haves Foreign Secretary .so weak and unstable as Lord Derby, but we can't help it. (Laughter.) The father of the present Lord Derby once made rather a good hit against the Liberal Ministry, to whom he was opposed, by telling them they were constantly med- dling and muddling foreign affairs. Now, the present Lord Derby has taught us that it is quite possible to muddle without meddling. (Cheers and laughter.) I think, notwithstanding that we have a Ministry of this kind, which is not according to our own choice and desire—we s ould have chosen a better if we could— (la eels tel)—that meetings such as this have had a large influence in modifying the policy both of the Prime mister and the Foreign Secretary. (Hear, hear.) I have no doubt at all that the Conference in London last Friday did an enormous amount of good in mollifying the anger which the Emperor of Russia must have felt when he found himself defied inso- lently by a fifth-rate novelist, from amongst the cups at the Guildhall. (Loud cheers and laughter.) I have so doubt whatever that what happened there has smoothed Lord Salisbury's course very much for him at that greater Conference which is now being held at Constantinople. (Hear, hear.) No doubt what was said by the statesmen who are outside the Government in reference to the pacific intentions and to the hon- ourable intentions of tho Emperor of Russia, must have had a very soothing effect upon ,the mind of the Emperor, and also upon the mind of his Ministevewho represent him at Constantinople. (Hear, hear.) Willa I believes great deal of good haa been done by meetings in this country daring the last few weeks we must remember that great watchfulness on the part of the people of this country is still required. (Hear, hear.) We believe that we have turned the course of , the Ministry from a bad and fatal one to a good and fortunate one; but we are not quite certain about it, and it is extremely desirable that meetings should still be held, and that this question should still be kept be- fore the attention of. the country, so that an influence for good may proceed from such meetings as we are holding to-night. (Hear, hear.) I have now only to Introduce to you Mr. Pollard, who will address you, and I ask for him, and for the remarks he will have to make, your attentive consideration. (Cheers.) Mr. W. rOLL/11D, who was received with cheers, gave an interesting historical account of the origin and re- Sults of the Crimean war. During the course of his remarks he said that some time ago when lecturing in the vicinity of Manchester, his chairman was the veteran reformer, Mr. Elijah Dixon, who had now passed away, snd he told the meeting that having pre- sided at a similar gathering during the reform agita- tion of 1832, he was arrested at the conclusion of the meeting, put in irons, and taken to London between two files of armed aoldiers. Now however, there was no fear that their esteemed chairman, Mr. MoMinnies, would be served like that. (Laughter.) In fact the thing was so outrageous that even "a fifth-rate no- velist" would not think of introducing it into hia story. (Laughter.) Reformers like Mr. Dixon had achieved for the people freedom and innumerable ! blessings which would have been unattainable but for the forty years peace which preceded the Crimean war. (Heat, hear.) Daring that time slavery was abolished, the trade and commerce of the nation had become fairly established, and civil and religious liberty had been obtained. He mentioned this to show that it was during the absence of war only that national progress could be attained. After dwelling on the folly of duelling, which he illustrated by ()abbot% characteristic refusal to accept a challenge, the lecturer condemned the " spirited " foreign Dolt" of the Government, and the folly of adopting foreign treaties, which wens broken as soon as made regardlese of their cost. They could not have a better instance of this than the treaty of Vienna, which it cost six hundred millions to obtain, one article of which was that no Napoleon should ever sit on the throne of France, and yet upon the late Emperor's accession in 1852, the English Foreign Minister was the first to conghterratu- .) late him upon the auspicious event. gatug The results of the Crimean war had been most disas- trous financially. It had caused an addition of ten millions a year to be made to our military expendi. tore, in our ignorance we had lent this precious Turk a few millions which we would never see agmn. (Laughter.) It had cost us 400 millions of pounds fs, which all the 16,000 miles of Railway in the kingdom could have been purchased. Why was all this sacrifice of men and money? All this had been done as Sir Wil- frid Lawson had said, to keep a wicked old swindler on his legs twenty years longer. (Laughter.) The difficulty was not yet over. All Europe was arming, influential nations were on the verge of bankruptcy through their military expenditure, and all because of the inordinate love of annexation. He presumed they had all heard of Mr. Charley (laughter)—who said that the members of the Peace Society advocated a war of extermination. He (the lecturer) wrote to Mr. Charley and asked AO mem- ber of the Peace Society said that, and in reply he said it was Mr. Peter Rylands, the member for Burnley, whom he supposed they all knew. Mr. Joint °BOMB= rose and said: I rise to move a vote of thanks to the lecturer for the able address he has delivered to us to-night, and I am sure lam speaking the feeling of every gentleman in the room when I say that we have listened to the lecture with interest and with instruction. (Hear, hear.) It is quite a treat to me to hear him recount so vividly the history of the Crimean war twenty years ago. It brought back to my memory scenes that happened when I was almost a lad. I went over to Manchester at the election of Gibson and Bright, who were fight- ing two Tory members, and I was in Newell's buildings when the result of the poll was announced, and it was that Gibson and Bright were thrown out. They were thrown out because they ads °cited peace and condemned war. (Hear, hear.) I remember Mr, Jacob Bright and Mr. Geo. Wilson saying that Newell's building baked more sit if there had been a funeral than anything else. 'twits utterly silenced,not a sound could be heard, and Mr. Jacob Bright made one of the noblest speeches I ever heard in my life. He said that he felt far more for Mr. Gibson than he did for his own brother, who was then out of the country, and he pro- phesied that the day would come when England would repent of her policy, and that Gibson and Bright would have their reward. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, the day has come. (Hear, hear.) We accept the opinions of John Bright as the most sensible opinions in England to-day. (Hear, hear.) He has never altered, beholds the same opinions now that he held twenty years ago. (Hear, hear.) He never made a finer speech in his life than he did at Birmingham last week, in which he exposed the false policy of this country in going into that Crimean war. (Hear, hear.) The only thing we have got to fear is that we have a Prime Minister at the head of the Government of this country who is a perfect disgrace to us. (Laugh- ter and cheers.) I declare I have not language to de- scribe him. (Laughter.) Ha is a man without a con- science, who for the sake of his own paltry glory would hurry this country into war. But if this Tory ministry attempt to go to war for these execrable Turks, I trust that every Englishman will rise as one man, and hurl the present administration from power. (Loud cheers.) I believe it will be done, and it will be a great blessing when the country is rid of such an unmitigated hypocrite as Lord Beaconsfield. (Laughter and cheers.) For a man occupying the position he does, to dare to stand up at the Guildhall, and make a speech which was intended to inflame the passions of the Russian people, and to precipitate war, there is no language too strong with which to denounce him. (Cheers.) I dare say you have heard of the Home bocretary, Mr. Assheton-Cross—most of you know him —(laughter)—who spoke at Birmingham, and he said .4 what minister in his senses would wish for war P" What did he mean? Did he mean that Lord Beacons- field was out of his senses. (Laughter.) Did he mean to say that Lord Beaconsfield was suffering from what they call a heated imagination, at nine o'clock at night, when he made that speech? (Laughter.) Be- cause I never in my life read a speech more indicative of a wish for war than that was. It made the whole of England distrustful and anxious, and caused a lot of meetings to be held, which showed that the opinion of , the English people was against the Prime Minister, and that we were for peace and not for war. (Cheers.) I have great pleasure iu moving a vote of thanks to the worthy lecturer for the splendid address he has given us. (Cheers.) div.head: CURIOUS ACCIDENT AT THE CHESHIRE HUNT.
div.p: A CURIOUS ACCIDENT AT THE CHESHIRE HUNT.

The Duke of Westminstet's groom met with a pain- ful accident on Saturday. His Grace and Lady Beatrice were in at the kill at Broughton, near Chester after a sharp spin with the Cheshire hounds, to they were riding away the horse which the Duke rode had the misfortune to run a piece of iron some distance into its hoof. His grace at once dismounted, and held the horse's head, while the groom proceeded to examine the animal's foot. The auimal gave a violent kick, the iron heel of the hoof striking the groom beneath the chin, and laying bim senseless on the road. His grace endeavoured to restore animation, and assietanee was sent to "the field" for a doctor, but failing in both, a carriage was procured and in this the man was re- moved to Eaton Hall, in an unconscious state.

SCHOOL TEACHERS MEETING AT BOWDON.

The annual meeting of the Church School managers and teachers Association, Bowdon District, was held on Saturday afternoon, in the Parish Church School- room. The Hon. W. Egerton, M.P. prodded, and there Were also present—the Rev. G. Heron, Rev. Canon Gore, Rev. R. Hodgson, Rev. G. London, Rev. H. Barnacle, Rev. F. Wainwright, Rev. J. Francis, Rev. C. V. Merriman, Mr. R. H. joynson, Mr. E. Collin, Mr. Tweedale, Mr. Hams, Mr. Stanley, Mr. Goodall, and Mr. H. W. Eves= (secretary.) The annual report showed a small increase in the number of members, and the balance sheet sheaved a email balance in hand. The CiLimms.st referred to the email attendance, and said he thought that if the Society was to be what . it ought to he, a reality, it ought not to be con- tinued if it was not. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GOODiLL read a paper on prize schemes. He advocated the persuasive means of educating the people rather than the oompulsOry, and suggested that prizes should be given for good attendance. He be- lieved children were put to work at too early an age, and at a time when their education was unfinished. The Rev. R. Honosorr, of St. Margaret's, Dunham, generally approved of the scheme, ea did also the Rev. G. HERON. Canon Goan suggested that the matter be referred to a committee. He thought they would be able to raise £lOO or £1.50 for the purposes suggested by the essayiat. He moved "that the whole question of whether it would be desirable to institute a prize scheme for the School Association be referred to the committee to report upon at the next meeting." Mr. Hams seconded the motion, and supported the 'views of the reader of the paper. The Rev. Gm. LONDON, of St. George Church, Al- trincham speaking of the National Schools, said that he had not the slightest doubt if they could trace the his- tory of a great many of their distinguished families they would find that they took their origin from some one member who was educated in those schools, and who by his talent and ability had got to the univer- sities and completed his education; whereas now he thought a great deal had been done by the Legislature really to rob the poor of this chance of making use of the talents God had endowed them with— (hear, hear) —and the class legislation had been in the direction of helping those who could help themselves. They vir- tually excluded all their boys from the grammar schools of the country, or if they went they were made so wretchedly uncomfortable that they could not remain there. If they were to help forward the educa- tion of the country and bring out the real talents among the poor, they would have some inducement to offer to the children to keep them at school, and he should like to see some large scheme set on foot, where they could hold out, to the boys particularly, some in- ducement to make use of their time and talents. There 'Mould be no impediments to their rising to the very highest positions that they were capable of occupying, and on that account he should be glad to see that subject ventilated and thoroughly considered. (Ap- plause.) Mr. R. H. JOYNSON, J.P., explained the system adop- ted in the Manchester Schools, and Ur. EVRION agreed with the Rev. Mr. London, and said that they had not any corporation to appeal to, but, while they had in Altrincham not exactly a cor- poration, they had a Mayor with large funds at his disposal, wh;ch might, he thought, if proper applica- tion were made, be forthcoming to found one of these exhibitions for some school in the neighbourhood, At all events, he thought the money would be forth- coming for the purpose. (Cheers.) The Rev. HY. Banar.soms, vicar of Rnutsford, sup- ported the resolution, and spoke in favour of higher education in the Church schools. Mr. STANLEY was in favour of annual examinations, instead of half-yearly ones, as he considered the latter great waste of time. gi The CLlAmigar thought that until they had farther the education Act, would be s seen prematureth the w otroknoginofto the scheme. He considered that the chief thing the committee would have to aim at would be to arrange a system of prizes or awards,tand as much as possible elicit the sympathy and co-Operation of the parents, in sending their children to school, and so prevent the compulsory powers of the Act being broughtinto use, as he trusted thedy never would be. They would next have to provi e,..t.ra which would admit of a gradual rise of the h"" eat boys in National Sshools to the Un4versities. He though that the prizes should be prizes of honour rather thit: of a pecuniary nature. In conclusion, he said, In thet present day there was a constant 4, cramming n for examinations. It was a result of the age. He con_ essed, having gone throught them himself, that public examinations were necessary itt.- pto a certain point. He thought, however, they might overdo them, and that they should not be kept in a constant state of high pressure in working up for examinations. (Hear, hear.) There was another thing which Was rather overlooked in the present day, viz., that it was not AlwaPi the clever boy at school that made the best an in after life—(applause)—and therefore any system which encouraged and brought forward those whose abilities might be very excellent, but whose moral character was not good was one which was not satisfactory, and in any system of prizes they should ever encourage it at the expense of moral conduct. (Cheers.)

MEETING' OF THE:ALTRINOHAIL TRADES COUNCIL.- - A tea and pubEc meeting, under the auspices of the Altrineliam Trades Council, was hold in the British Schoolroom, Altrincham, on Wednesday evening. There was a fair attendance. Mr. Bell presided, and amongst those present there were Mr. Thomas Holli- day, Mr. J. D. Prior, Mr. Henry R. Slater, &o. The CHAIRMAN, Mr. F. T. Bell, said that he had re- ceived letters of apology from two gentlemen, Mr. Robert Last, raid Mr. Peter Shorrocks, who were un- able to be present. After paying a high compliment to some of the gentlemen on the platform, he said that the Trades Council intended to submit to the meeting two resolutions, one in favour of the Workmen's Com- pensation Bill and the other in favour of the assimila- tion of the county and borough franchise. With respect to the first, so far as he understood it, all the workingmen required was, that reasonable care and precaution should be taken, so that men in following their usual employment should not be maimed or killed, and that m the event of contractors or masters being guilty of negligence the workingmen in their employ should be compensated for injuries so brought about. With regard to the County Franchise, it was a matter which he had given attention to for years, , and he confessed that the more he examined into the matter, the more he was struck with the injustice of the present system of representation. He could not understand how it was that men living in boroughs should be entitled to vote, whilst one living in the county and occupying a similar position, paying the same rates and taxes, should be debarred from enjoy- ing the privilege. They had been told that it did not matter whether they had votes or not, as they were represented by the county members. He denied that; it required two parties to make a bargain, as they had no share in electing a representative they denied that they were represented. Which of the county members would vote for the dieestablishment of the Church, an amendment of the land laws, game laws, or any others which require amandment and tax labour. They were told that they were too ignorant to vote too poor and too low and too degraded to vote. If that were so the best thing to do was for them to amend their condi- tion. He should like to know whether those who had the franchise in the county were paragons of wisdom? He ventured to say that a large number of those now possessing the vote in the counties and boroughs were numekulls' and therefore their ignorance was no bar to their vote. They took their stand on the broad and unassailable principle, taxation, which without re- presentation was a gross injustice. Whether they were too poor and too low to vote or not, they, the working men, had made this great nation what it is. (Applause.) They had fought this country's battles by land and sea, yet the brothers and fathers of such men were not allowed to exercise the privilege of direct representation. They enjoyed the great privilege of helping to pay the piper, yet they would not let them enjoy the music, (Laughter.) They desired to enter a most serious, earnest, and solemn protest against that, and to tell the Government and the members of Parliament, and all opponents to the extension of the suffrage, that the present arrange- ment was vicious, unnatural, and unjust in principle. (Hear, hear,) The growing intelligence of the masses would be too much for them, and the lines of demar- cation between the county and borough franchises Iwrowu lads for b eforce hoof h publicaa rh c poopwineiroonf, making and unmakiug members of Parliament, whom ts hwoeepeti n awayt h bboyr ot uh .. they looked to for aeaistance in that matter. He ex- horted them to work on with undiminished zeal a.cl unflinching energy, strengthened and supported by the thought that they were working in a good and just cause, and the grand old cause of liberty, justice, and freedom. (Cheers.) MT. SGIINSON MILLINGTON moved—" That in the opinion of this meeting the law relating to the com- pensation to workmen who meet with accidents while following their usual employment is in a most unsatis- factory state, and that therefore this meeting desires the members who represent this division of the county in the House of C0D3.1110118 to support the principles embodied in Mr. Macdonald's bill of last session." MT. RD. WALTON seconded the motion, anel MT. BLATTHII supported it, and contended that workmen ought to have provision for accidents resulting from the carelessness of other people, as was the case when accidents arose to men not in their employ. That, they said, was A gross and palpable injustice, (Hear, hear.) Mr. THOMAS HALLIDAY, secretary of the Amalga- mated Society of Miners, in supporting the resolution, said Lord Campbell's Act, although it provided for com- pensation to persons injured by another person's negli- gence, it excepted workmen. In the case of railway companies, they were responsible for the safety of the passengers, although in the ease of their own servants there was no such legal obligation. They (the people with whom he was most intimately con- nected—the miners) were subject to very great in- juries indeed through explosions and falls of earth. It had caused them to take action against the mine owners for compensation in cases where men were sacrificed through the carelessness or in- difference of the colliery proprietors. They were de. termined, if possible, to compel mine owners, if they permitted the unnecessary netlike of husbands and brothers, to keep their widows and children. The law made no such provision at present, on behalf of work- men, and workmen were the only persons who could not recover in a Court of law compensation for injuries received, through another e carelessness. The members of Parliament would do what they were made, and no more. Mr. MacDonald's bill only sought to procure on behalf of the working classes the same priveleges which were enjoyed by the other part of the com- munity. When Ur. Macdonald was speaking in the House of Commons in favour of his bill, Mr. Cross the Home secretary was obliged to admit that the present state of the law was not satisfactory, and he promised that if Mr. Macdonald would not press his motion, he would appoint a select committee. (Hear. hear.) They wanted the law equal and fair to all alike, yet the masters were trying to prevent this, and throughout the country they had set their faces against the working men. The mine owners had an organization throughout the land, and they were trying to get up evidence to shew that the men had no case. It was their business to show that they had. If they, the workmen were well backed up by the members of Parliament, their claims would be pro• perly considered, and they would get their rights. Mr. Knowles, M.P., for Wigan had been vile enough to say over and over again—and he had denied it as often—that if the compensation laws were changed, there were men bad enough to allow themselves to be injured for the purpose of receiving compensation. (Shame.) He (the speaker) never heard a viler attack against the workingmen. (Applause.) He contended Oat had proper precautions been taken, the colliery explosion in Monmouthshire would not have taken place. He believed that if proper precautions were taken 75 per cent. of the accidents might be avoided. They said that if the masters would wink their eyes and would not look after those things—under or above ground, and permitted their men to be inj tired by neg- lect of officers or officials—they intended to try and get the law so altered that they might be proceeded against, and made to pay for such negligence and carelessness. PRIOB, chairman of the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Congress, said that the reso- lution he was called upon to support did not require much to be said on its behalf. He had no doubt that all workingmen felt the inequality of the present fran- chise, and had made up their minds to have it altered. At a political demonstration in London some nine and a half years ago, they had the words which was after- wards used by Mr. John Bright, in one of his histori- cal speeches, which were—" Deal with us on the square, you have chiselled us long enough." HOW THEY LIVE AND DIE IN WARRINGTON. At an inquest on Monday before Mr. Driffield on the body of a child aged 11 days which was found dead at its mother's breast, the jury had occasion to visit the residence of the chill's mother, Bridget Flynn in Kinder's Yard.—ln answer to questions by the jury, the woman stated that she paid 3s. a week for the house in which she lived. There was one room downstairs and one upstairs. Herself, husband, the baby, and three children slept in this room. None of the other children slept in the same bed as she was in with the infant, but they slept on the floor. Several of the jurymen described the state of the houses in Kinder's Yard as being disgraceful to any town. The houses jiad only two rooms, and they were in a most filthy slate, and not fit for human habitation. They thought that the attention of the Nuisance Inspector should be called .to them,—The Coroner said that from the appearance of the witnesses he could believe all that had been said; but this was not a matter for him, but for their legal authorities. They as inhabitants of the town ought to try and get them done away with.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child had died from natural causes, and probably from convulsions.

"SABBATARIANISAI-IN THE YEAR OF GRACE 1876."

The Rev. H. W. Perris delivered a special discourse on the above, topic, to a large congregation, in Cairo-st. Chapel, Warrington, last Sunday evening. A selection of scriptural passages was read during the service, with the object chewing the vicissitudes which Sabbath observance had undergone since the great Jewish legislator had established it. Mr. Perrin prefaced his address by reading Col. ii., 16, and Romans xii., 6, 6. • Sabbatarianiem" was defined as the consecration of a period of time (variously measured and named) to exclusive religious uses, and the idea necessarily im- plied an entire abstinence from labour and pleasure. Abroad, he had witnessed the observance of three con- secutive Sabbaths in each week, Friday being the Mohammedan, Saturday the Jewish, and Sunday the Christian day of rest. In Sootland, until the rigour of Calvinism began to abate under the growing in- fluence of science and literature, the Sabbath wae en- forced by the clergy with Hebrew strictness. N o fires were lit ; the very clocks were often stopped because they broke the solemn stillness of the holy day. Dean Ramsay gave some capital illustrations of this bondage to the letter of the old law. Here, in England, our principles and practices were alike anomalous. We partly recognised and partly ignored the freedom from " ordinances " vihich Jesus and Paul had so passion- ately vindicated against the Sabbatarians of their day. Our legislation and our 'national usages were very composite, because our growth had been interrupted by revolutions which had encouraged "the falsehood of extremes." From the Sunday sports of Charles to the everlasting sermon-hearing of Puritan time% was a wide leap indeed. How stood the case to-day ? New legislation was called for by the new needs. In- telligent religious men were beginning to see that the mass of the people could no longer he induced to " sanctify " the first day of the week by an appeal to oldeworld tradition about the creation of the world in six days, and the "rest" of the Holy One on the seventh. Science gloriously amplified and illustrated the de- claration of the prophet that "He fainteth not, neither is weary," and shows Christ's new commandment to be wiser and truer than the old regulative code. Our " Father worketh hitherto," pausing not in his plan, but ceaselessly impelling man along the lines of progress. Hes, then,' the old Jewish prohibition no force? None whatever to those who have "put away childish things," and learned that the son of man is lord even of the Sabbath day. The dimly lighted con- science has its rights, and must not he interfered with ; as St. Paul says, " He that observeth the day observeth it to the Lord." But the liberated and enlightened conscience has also its rights ; " He that observeth not the day, to the Lord he observeth it not." The law of the land cannot now be suffered to press on the reli- gious liberty of more than half a community. Coming to the matter of recent prosecution, and the threats of the Head Constable that buyers as well as sellers should be prosecuted, Mr. Perris contended that the action of the Watch Committee was as un- wise as it was oppressive. He was told by the magisratee whom he had consulted, that the real object in view was a sanitary one, and that it was not intended really .to execute the threats which bad been tittered against the small shopkeepers Could such a crooked policy as that serve the turn of law, order, and religion? He was not prepared to con- demn the selling of cheap meat on Sunday morning to the poor, who, perhaps could not attar(' to pay the regular price on Saturday. But if it were wrong and dangerous to the health of the community, it was the business of the sanitary committee to eal with it, Why evoke an obsolete Sabbeth-law, when the magis • trates themselves regularly "profaned tbe Sabbath and were held blameless F" Was there one law for the rich and another law for the poor? And were the people to be driven into more thorough-going revolt against Christianity than ever, at the bidding of some Dogberry with more zeal than knowledge? Turning to the positive aspects of the 'region, Mr. Perris said the true law of periodical rest and recreation was written in the nerve and muscle and brain of man. As the people got wiser they would refuse to be the sieves of either Mammon or Conventional Orthodoxy, There Would continue to -be a class living on the verge of pogerty and from hand to mouth, and no Sabbath law could Prevent that. Let the dithers of the peace enforce the law against them who make the people drunk on Saturday n;ght, and there would be fewer buyers and sellers ou Sundays. And, let the need of intelleotael refreshment on the Sunday be receguised. For his own part, he trusted. God would give him strength to stir up the oonseienoe of the community, an: advocate the opening of the Museum, the Library, and the new Art Gallery for a few hours on Sunday afternoon, that some of the people might be tempts I out of their alleys into the precincts of the little temple of know- ledge in Bold-street, and there learn that there were "near and heavenly horizens" of tru'h and love to which no Sabbath bells had yet won them r

THE REV, GEORGE KENNEDY'S LECTURE ON "ROBERTSON." The last of the preliminary series of lectures for the people, prier to the commencement of the science lectures, took place in the Public Hall on Monday tremble, the lecturer being the Rev. Geo. Kennedy, and his subject "Frederick William Robertson, of Brighton; preacher, thinker, and critic." There Wii6 a tolerably good audience considering the inclemency of the weather. In introducing the lecturer, fdr. C. Bnoxnexue, who occupie I the chair, said he felt bound, on behalf of those present of the general public' of Warrington, to thank those gentlemen who had so kindly volunteered to instruct and entertain them by their lectures. Mr. Kennedy had that night chosen a most interesting sub. jact, viz., the life and writings of a man who had per. naps b en influenced by the religious thought of the present day more than any men living. The Rev. Mr. KENNEDT, who was heartily received, Bald: Some 20 or 24 years ago, Frederick William Robertson began to make himself felt among us as a power. He had died leaving behind him a well-earned reputation of a profound thinker, a noble-gentleman and a high-souled public teacher. Progressive in- tellects mierel a living presence which had helped them in their struggles. Earnest hearts felt that a leading light was quenched, and that the world was darker for its loss, and men began to accord him a foremost place in the ranks of later gifted Englishmen. Some knows ledge of his life and genius has become necessary. He wields over our intellect and feeliog an influence unsurpassed by that of any other living teacher. His views of centre truths are permeating otir religious thought. His expositions determine permanently the views of many aspiring students. Not a few authors are proud to call him master, aud never contradict him without letting it be seen how unwillingly they de- parted from such a leader. He is the exponent of ideas which had long been maturing in a limited circle of advanced thinkers. New phases and illustration: of truth, and certain speculative impulses have ob. tamed a footing mainly through his adopting theta. He is one whose doubts, beliefs, and culture touch upon our own. Some of us have lived over the same period, studied the same authors, and shared the same experience. After giving an interesting sketch of hie college life and associasions, Mr. Kennedy alluded to the part played by Keble and Neuman in bringing about the Ritualistio movement. Robertson, after fairly discussing the matter, felt that he must adhere to evangelical opinions, and could not join himself to 'the measures of a school which exhausts its fervour in ceremonials, and a Tractarian he never became. Nor did he merely fortify himself against it. He assailed It as the Oxford delusion-heresy ; predicted the curse of heaven on it, and headed an association to counter. act it. Still he did not join in the slander with which Its leaders were attached. At a time when brave speaking was at a discount, he spoke right bravely of their manlinsss and practical work. To the end he read Newman's sermons with delight, end held no book in higher esteem than the " Christian Year." Mr. Robertson's rebound was as much from Newman personally as from his school. Aldre imbued with speculative tendeno es, and having between them so much common ground on which to meet, they yet be- came typieel in their divergence. From Oxford, Robertson passed into active life. His first curacy was Winchester, where he found the people rude and somewhat empties]. But his beautiful voice, his dig. Lifted yet vivid action, his impassioned fervour, and the bright enthusiasm which he brought to bear upon theological questions, soon rooted him in their esteem. After fully describing his work at Winchester, at Cheltenham, and afterwards as incumbent of an Ox- ford parish, the rev. lecturer came to Robertson's removal to Brighton, and said it was by his seven years' work there that he would be remembered. 110. terrine to the change in Robertson from Evanzelloal to Broad Church principles, the lecturer said this change In Robertson had been a puzzle to his critics; but to his mind they had not gone far enough back ie seeking to explain it. With reference to his preaching, the lecturer said that public opinion was divided about the brilliant man. Some psople missing routin phrases, and suepecting heresy, fled the church. Another party e reported him to the bishop for preaching politics, and bespattered him with such terms as atheist, pantheist, and revolutionist. Still his church went on filling. Thinkers came Gemmed by the ring of truth. The curious came, drawn by matchless imagery and rapid rushing eloquence. Young men were allured by his del cate analyses of the human heart; the artisans came, accenting of his lectures as an honest eft srt to solve, in Christian pi inciples, the problems which per. plexed them. And there came by shoals men who were never previously seen in a church. His most visible success was amongst the working class, and beeanee he sought to makelhem truer men, better workmen, wiser Englishmen, he built himself a noble monument in their hearts. After describing, in an exhauAive manner, all his virtues and characteristics, the rev, lecturer concluded the first part of his address by saying—" I cannot think of him without regercting him as the advocate in this country of what is termed ' liberal theology.' He actei under an irelletence, which, call it g_enius, or, enthusiasm, or mental seem. tion. indisposed ,hion to abide by the old landmarks of religious thought. His is the theology of an age of questioning and earnest aspiration, essentially intel. lectual and philosophic. It is a conflict between conventionalism and sincerity; between rationalism and unintelligible faith; between idealism and mate. rialism. In it we see men not in his art anl eisulless mechanism, but in his orisisethroes. We see into his nature, its passions, discords, storms, and unrest, and hunger after higher tru.h." The rev, lecturer then dwelt at length upon Robertson as a thinker and as a critic, and gave some eloquent illustrations from Robertson's writings, which were highly appreciated by the audience. At the close of the lecture, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Me. liennody for his iuterestiog lecture.

div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECAMBER 23, 1876.

THE REGISTRAR OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES AND TRADES 'UNIONS. Tun Registry of Friendly Societies was placed on a new footing in 1875, and the chief Registrar of such Societies. Mr. J. M. Ludlow who was appointed under the Act of that year, has just published a printed report of what has come into his office in the way of registration of Friendly Societies, during that year. Trade Unions have since, by an Amendment Act of last Session come within his purview, and all are subordinated to a very stringent supervision by the Lords of the Treasury, by which the Chief Regis- trar seems reduced to a position of a head clerk, who may receive all kinds of applica- tions, but may decide upon none without the consent of 'My Lords.' The registry office appears by the report before us, to do a great deal of work, but as a commercial enterprise it is, we sadly fear, uneuccessful. The Chief-Registrar and his staff of about a dozen, :have their salaries paid by the Treatniry, and the fees received by the Chief Registry are paid over into the Ex- chequer, which is, we presume, another name for the Treasury. The total of these fees amount to nearly £6OO a year, a sum rather less we should imagine than would content the Chief-Registrar in the matter of salary. The staff of the registry office has not been greatly increased in consequence of the additional labour thrown upon it. Another copying clerk has been authorised to be employed, and the only other addition to the staff has been realized in the person of a messenger, a gentleman whose em- ployment is probably to bring in luncheon at one o'clock, put some coals on the fire now and then, and take the letters to the post when all is done, and the office closes at four o'clock in the afternoon. The business transacted in the Chief Re- gistry ;is the registering and certifying of rules of Friendly Societies, of Industrial and Provident„, otherwise called Co-operative Societies, of Building Societies, of Trade Unions, and of Loan Societies. The Regis- trar notices that the number of Friendly Societies registered was smaller than in the previous year, and that, he adds, was below the average. He proposes to account for this by the fact that legislation on the sub- ject was pending during both years; we cannot however see that this is any satisfac- tory reason, or that he is at all called upon to suggest any reason for it. We might say with equal probability that there are Friendly .Societies enough at present, for they are not registered afresh every year, or that people's experience of them is not satis- factory, and they don't want any more, or that they prefer to put their savings into Building Societies, of which the report states there is a large increase, but how large that increase is does not ',clearly appear, as the number given includes Building Societies which were previously existing under certi- fied rules, and have now by a re-registration been obtaining a, certificate of, incorporation under the Act of 1874.

Like other organised beings, Friendly So- cieties are liable to the process of dissolu- tion. In 1876 the Chief Registrar noticed 47 which had dissolved of their own free will, and had advertised the fact in the London Gazette, Four others had been dis- solved by the Registrar Lou the ground of insolvency. The only true basis of friend- ship has been defined to be mutual useful- ness, and here was an instance of the truth of the definition—the usefulness having ceased the friendly .character of the union vanished. Another and a rather mysterious mode of dissolution seems to be accomplished by sending a letter to the Registrar. 'Twenty- nine societies performed their happy despatch by this method—three of them we find are in Lancashire, a Female Temperance Society in Manchester, an Oddfellows Lodge, of the " united" species, in Liverpool, and an Orange Benefit Lodge at Bootle; the last we can certainly say causes us no surprise, for we cannot imagine an Orange Society being of benefit to anybody, except to the tapster who supplies the drink. The governing power of the Treasury, which we have before referred to, seems to make that and not the Registry the real office for the transaction of business. The Chief Registrar is appointed by the Trea- sury, and they may appoint an Actuary, though they have not yet done so, and neither the Registrar nor Actuary is to pub- lish any forms of balance sheets, valuations, annuity tables, or the like, without the ap- proval of the Treasury; and the consent of the Treasury is required before the Regis- trar can determine a dispute, and they have also decided that any further clerks wanted must uudergo a competitive examination ' under the regulations of the Civil Service Commissioners. "On the other hand," the Registrar humorously observes, "the situa- tion of charwoman in the Registry of Friendly Societies' office has been, by an order of Council of 4thjune, 1870, exempted from the necessity of a preliminary examination of candidates before the Civil Service Commissioners," but N. B. he adds in parenthesis, "There is at present no charwoman in the office, but only a 'caretaker' appointed by the officer of works." Who shall say after this that there is no amusement to be got out of a Parlia- mentary Blue-Book? div.head: CONFERENCE AT CONSTANTINOPLE.
div.p: THE CONFERENCE AT CONSTANTINOPLE.

THE vague and nebulous condition of affairs at Constantinople previous to the advent thither of Lord Salisbury is said to contrast in a striking manner with the rapid growth of a common understanding between the re- presentatives of the European Powers. Per- haps it would be mole accurate to speak rather of to " desire " to arrive at a common understanding on the part of these plenipo- tentiaries. The birth of a spirit of mutual conciliation and the dissipation of much of the traditional distrust with which the action of the great powers have baen heretofore impeded or paralysed, seems to be relieving the gloom in which tho Eastern question has been so long enveloped. All that is at pre- sent possible to say, however, in referring to Turkish affairs, is that the aspect of things is distinctly hopeful. Turkey seems at last to be able to cpmprehend that what is called its " integrity " will not, under all or any cir- cumstances, be maintained by the blood and money of the people of England. It has been well said that the newypapers in this country which affect to wish Lord Salisbury's mission to succeed, and yet assure the Turk that if it should fail, and the Conference come to nothing, England would still be their friend, and that 'their enemies would be hers. It is incontestible that this is a bad service to render to our own Govern- ment, but a worse to render to that of Tur- key. The event of the week of most con- siderable significance is perhaps that of the deposition of the Turkish Prime Minister in favour of a new Grand Vizier—Midhat Pacha, the Minister who elaborated the new Constitution, with which the Porto seemed desirous of anticipating European in- tervention. In any paper Constitution of the Porte there is now as little confidence amongst European Governments, as, it is said, there is in Turkey itself. Even if Turkish honesty in this matter was above suspicion, it is believed that the Porte is powerless to accomplish the necessary Ireforms. It is alleged that local influence is omnipotent, and would, and could, defeat the intentions of the most honest administra- tions. This being so, it is felt that Europe can have no guarantee against the recurr- ence of Bulgarian horrors, and the assur- ance that the christian populations of Turkey I will be treated with common humanity and fairness, in the absence of a military occupa- tion of one kind or another. Every day the Journals afford glimpses of the dismal dis- tresses of the populations, condemned to the yoke of Turkey. At the meeting of the Bulgarian Relief Committee, hold in Man- chester on Wednesday, a telegram was read from Mr. Long, who is administering the fund in the distressed districts. Mr. Long says he has been successful beyond his highest hopes, but "the sad truth is that the funds provided are totally inadequate to accomplish the enormous task " set before him. The Committee have received £7,455. Belgium has been mentioned as a country free from the possiblity of sinister designs in the East. The correspondent of the Daily News in Berlin telegraphs that it is understood there that Belgium would refuse to under- take the occupation of Bulgaria, even if requested by the Powers. From Constan- tinople information comes in the same sense. It is added that Switzerland has already declined. A reported prolongation of the armistice has been contradicted. A telegram from St. Petersburgh states that nothing is known in official quarters there of it. In the event of the prolongation taking place, it is said that the Plenipotentiaries at Constan- tinople have decided that it will be neces- sary to fix a line of demarcation in Bosnia, and to effect this a Consul and a military commissioner will be sent by each of the Powers,

To repeat; the aspect of Turkish affairs is less discouraging than a few weeks ago, but the difficulties of the situation are still enormous. The fact is that the Porte is awakening to the certainty that English blood and English taxes can no longer be counted upon to sustain the moral and material anarchy of an effete system of ad- ministration.

Perhaps the youthfulness of Dr. McKerrow, boddy as well as mentally, i to the general observer his most remarkable characteristic. We accept men who are known to be advanced in years in that advanced sense. We accept the= as being older than we are ourselves, and older to an extent which we do not care to compute. Old boy—old cock—old doctor. Those arc our familiar and by no means disrespectful cogno- mens. Now, in the first place, Dr. Alclierrow, in his seventy-fourth year, does not look old. He is grizzled, but not hoary. The rubicund complexion liAhts up the grizzlement, and, to a great extent, effaces it. Our dear doctor (God bless him, we delight to write about him), with an obstinate Scotch valour, stands out against Time, which cannot work any wrinkle 3 on his azure brow—which does not so far shrivel up his figure or take off its roundness, or develops knocked less in the knees, or attenuation at the back of the neck. A youthful garotter, for instance, "trying it on " with the doctor at Bowdon on a dark night would have to mind what he was about, b •cause peradventure, if the reverend gentlemen turned round and got his umbrella free, the youthful garotter would pro- bably have the umbrella first rammed down his throat and then opened out—rather an awkward " poszstion," as the doctor would say, for the youth- ful garotter

The career of Dr. B.l.Kerrow is almost indissolubly associated with the public, history of Blanchester for the last thirty years—may indeed be said to illustrate the history of Manoheeter durmg that period. Our own recollections of the good doctor ran nearly along- side the reminiscences of the principal speakers at the Refoim Club. . . .

Like Mr. Jacob Bright, we first krew, Dr. McKer. row as a public man at the time of the Auti-Coru Law League, and always regarded him as tho secogoised chaplain of that unequalled confederacy. The ban- quets (so called) of the League used to consist princi- pally of sandwiches and almonds and raisins, and we nurtured our politics then upon those modest condi- ments almost as well as we do now—probably better— upon turtle soup. The Doctor used to ask a blessirg upon the sandwiches and the almonds awl raisins, and occasionally he was in the habit of taking off his coat for a round or two with the Protectionists ou Lis own account, and of smiting them with quite an Old Te,ta- meat fervour as if he were dealing with the Hivites, the Hittites, and the Jebusites. . . .

Afterwards we got the Doctor in a milder form durir g some years of tea dining at the old Examiner 01nU,3. in what may be termed the pre-Duackley period' when the then editor, the late Mr. Paulton, used to enter the editorial arena, twice a week only, with amazing enthusiasm and abundant snuff, awl used to lecture Mr. Ireland, Mr. Peacock, Dr. Mcliarrow, and another whom modesty forbids us to mention, on the Philosophy of the Unconditioned and other practical tubjeots—as a steadier for leae.er writing.

Then again we encountered Dr. lliclin.row at the Lancashire Public School Association, in which Non- conformity played so laggard a part—the Doctor nevertheless seeing througa and through the question even then, and not being deceived; and, upon the question of elementary education, never having bet:.a deceived unto this day. But we must not attempt to go through the catalogue so well warn by the speakers on Monday evening. Tune would fail us if we were to attempt to write all the achievements of that active life. We Will only say thst as pastor, preacher, as publioi3t,philantrophist—steadfast in e faith of our Nonconforming forefathers, always in its wider and never in its narrower developments, stead- fast in the cause of civil an religions liberty the world over, he whom on Monday evening we met to honour should be an ensample to all of us; and tee rejoice exceedingly that instead of firing oratorical volleys over his grave we were enabled to Ist him see all this with his own eyes, and hear it with his own ears, and that the pulses of his own warm heart might beat more warmly in living response to the honour, love, and °bedience of those troops of friends.
J F. T.

A labourer named Thomas Dainteth was brought up under a warrant and charged with deserting his children ' and leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union, Mr. Fogg, the relieving dicer, stated that the defendant only came out of gaol In October last where he had been serving six months at Kirkdale for neglecting his children. He positively refused to maintain them, and had cost the union about £2OO. THE VAGARIES OF A VAGRANT.

A. tramp named John Connor was brought up in custody and charged with refusing to perform his allotted task of work, and also with breaking down his cell. It appeared that the prisoner refused to break stones, which is the usual task of vagrants, on the ground that he had rheumatism in his arm and desired to see the doctor. That official discovered the tramp was shamming, and when he found that he would be de- tained until he had finished his task, he seized a sledge hammer, and with ir. knocked down the wall or his cell and escaped. However his eight was observed, and when scaling the workhouse wall he was captured and brought back to the cells. The prisoner's defence was he could not break the stones, and that the Work- house was more like a prison than a place where an " unfortunate workingman " could get relief. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for two months with hard labour.

OUR CHRISTMAS: The leaves have left Dunham, the ferns have died down, The scant fronds remaining are stunted and brown, The trees are so listless, the nests are left bare, The branches seem lifeless, and poised in Mid-air. The walks through the woodlands are sodden and wet. But their glories in summer we cannot forget; The fields are forsaken—bereft of their corn The roads are untravell'd, the parks look forlorn. But down in .tbe hollow our old country town.* Is like a young maiden donned in her best gown, With red-berried holly, and arch mistletoe, Disputing your passsage wherever you go. There are mansions in Bowdon must be supplied, And dinners and balls o'er the whole country side, And smaller home gatherings, where hearts are as warm, And welcomes as hearty, untrammell'd by form. The shops are ablaze with an army of lights, And judged by the gazers are wonderful sights; Whatever the weather—if snowy or wet, Yule tide with the same preparation is met. A crooked, and queer, and mis-shapen old town, By.' charter" and " charity " worth its renown; With little municipal dignity here, It looks most important, at least once a year. It is not patronised by grandee or peer, But it elbows its way well year after year; And the "oldest inhabitant," proud of his name, Can scarcely believe the old town is the same. Its troubadour days are departed and dead, But it has " musieians " and " minstrels " instead; And they serenade" Christians" under the moon. A month before Christmas, regardless of tune. And brave men in' scarlet" at once make "a raid," On all '6 stores or arsenals" open for trade; They prize "Christmas prizes," and eat Christmas fare, In a way with any such town to compare. So God grant our Christmas may long be upheld, In " peace and goodwill," by none other excell'd ; A health to our "charter," God bless our old town, And may Christian charity guard its renown.
